title: Tuition-Free Community College
resolution: Resolved: States should make community college tuition-free.
summary: Tennessee and other states cover community college tuition for recent high school graduates. Should every state do it?

background.p: Since 2015, Tennessee Promise has covered community college tuition and fees left after other grants for students who enroll right after high school, keep at least a 2.0 GPA, work with a mentor and do community service. More than 200 "promise" programs now exist across the U.S., with varying rules.

A 2025 working paper by economists Celeste Carruthers and Paige Schoonover, reported by Higher Ed Dive, found Tennessee Promise raised college enrollment among 19-year-olds by 5.4 percentage points and associate degrees among 21-year-olds by 2.9 points, increased transfers to four-year colleges, and raised early-career earnings by 6 to 8%. Because most students already qualify for Pell Grants or state aid, the program cost under $1,000 per participating student a year; one author said it pays for itself through higher earnings. Results of other promise programs vary.

disputed.q: Does free tuition raise graduation, or mostly enrollment?
positions: Tennessee's results show gains in both enrollment and degrees.
Critics note completion rates at community colleges remain low and that tuition is often not the main barrier; results differ across programs.

terms.def: Covers whatever tuition remains after other grants, like Pell Grants, are applied.
Covers tuition before other aid, so grants can go to living costs.
Federal grant aid for students from lower-income families.
The share of students who finish a degree or certificate within a set time.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Tuition-free community college opens doors to degrees and better jobs at a modest cost.

args.claim: Free tuition gets more students into college.
args.warrant: A clear promise of "free" is easier to understand than aid forms, and it reaches students who assume college isn't for them.
args.evidence: Carruthers and Schoonover: a 5.4-point rise in enrollment among 19-year-olds in Tennessee.
args.response: The negative answers that getting students in the door isn't enough if many don't finish.

args.warrant: More students who enroll and finish credentials earn more, which helps them and the state's economy.
args.evidence: Tennessee Promise: associate degrees up 2.9 points; earnings 6 to 8% higher in early adulthood; more transfers to four-year colleges.
args.response: The negative replies that one state's results may not carry over, and other programs show smaller effects.

args.warrant: Because federal and state grants already cover much tuition, a last-dollar promise costs relatively little per student.
args.evidence: Under $1,000 per participating student per year in Tennessee, as reported by Higher Ed Dive.
args.response: The negative argues last-dollar designs give little to the poorest students, whose tuition is already covered, while first-dollar designs cost much more.

args.claim: Workforce needs call for more trained workers.
args.warrant: Many growing jobs need a certificate or associate degree, and community colleges train nurses, technicians and tradespeople.
args.evidence: Bureau of Labor Statistics projections by education level; state workforce reports.
args.response: The negative replies that apprenticeships and employer-paid training may meet those needs more directly.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Free tuition spends money on the wrong barrier; aid should target need and completion.

args.claim: Tuition isn't the main barrier for low-income students.
args.warrant: Pell Grants already cover community college tuition for many low-income students; their bigger obstacles are living costs, work hours and child care.
args.evidence: Data on Pell Grant amounts and community college tuition; surveys of why students leave college.
args.response: The affirmative answers that the simple message of "free" still raises enrollment, as Tennessee shows.

args.claim: Benefits flow to families who could pay.
args.warrant: Last-dollar programs give the most money to students who don't qualify for need-based aid, often from middle- and higher-income families.
args.evidence: Analyses of who receives promise-program dollars by income.
args.response: The affirmative replies that middle-income families also struggle with costs, and universal programs win broad support.

args.warrant: Students who enroll and leave without a credential may end up with lost time and no payoff; money for advising and support may do more.
args.evidence: Community college completion data; studies of advising programs such as CUNY ASAP.
args.response: The affirmative replies that Tennessee's program includes mentoring and raised degrees, not just enrollment.

args.warrant: Dollars for free tuition can't go to K–12 schools, need-based aid or apprenticeships, which may help more students per dollar.
args.evidence: State budget data; evaluations of alternative workforce programs.
args.response: The affirmative argues the program's low cost and higher earnings mean it may pay for itself.

strawmen.strawman: They think everyone should get a free ride for everything.
strawmen.why: Most proposals cover only community college tuition, with requirements like GPA and mentoring.
strawmen.steelman: A clear promise of free community college raises enrollment, degrees and earnings at modest cost, as Tennessee shows.

strawmen.strawman: They don't want poor kids to go to college.
strawmen.why: Opponents favor aid targeted to need and to completion.
strawmen.steelman: Tuition isn't the main barrier for most low-income students; money should target living costs, advising and completion instead of tuition for families who can pay.

weak.arg: Free college means no one will have student debt.
weak.why: Living costs and four-year degrees still create debt; overclaiming invites an easy answer.
A slogan, not evidence; Tennessee's results contradict it.

aff: Does your plan cover tuition before or after Pell Grants?
What happens to students who enroll but don't finish?
Do other promise programs show the same results as Tennessee?
neg: What did the Tennessee study find about degrees and earnings?
How much did it cost per student?
What would you fund instead, and what evidence supports it?
